INFANT 2 · LESSON 4

First Words & Familiar Things for Babies 4–6 Months

Age 4–6 MonthsSubject TalkClass Infant 2Duration 2–5 minutes

Around four to six months, babies babble back, laugh at familiar faces and start to connect the sounds you make with the things they see. This class uses eleven simple familiar-object flashcards — a ball, a cup, a spoon, a bottle, an apple, a banana, a cat, a dog, a bird, a car and a teddy bear — shown one at a time while you name what you see in your own words.

There is no script and nothing to test. You talk, your baby listens, and the little everyday names — ball, cup, dog, hello — slowly grow into your baby’s first words. Short, calm sessions of two to five minutes are all it takes.

PARENT INSTRUCTIONS

How to use this activity

Choose a time when your baby is awake, calm and comfortable. Show one picture at a time and name what you see using simple, natural language. For example, say ‘ball’ or ‘Here is the ball.’ Give your baby time to look and listen.

Repeat words naturally, smile, and respond to your baby’s sounds and expressions. There is no need to test your baby or expect them to say the words.

Keep the activity short and stop when your baby looks away, becomes tired or loses interest.

Every baby develops differently. Kiddo School age ranges are guides, not tests or developmental deadlines.

TRY TOGETHER

Little things to say.

Prompts for you, not for the cards — say them softly while your baby looks.

  • Ball. Look at the ball.
  • Here is your cup.
  • Can you see the dog?
  • Hello, baby!

    Ball — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Few first words have a head start like this one: the ball is probably already your baby’s favourite toy. This lesson rolls the real thing into view and lets the fun carry the name.

    What is this?

    A ball is a round toy that rolls, bounces and stops — and your baby has probably already chased one with their eyes and hands. The card gives that favourite a clean portrait; the game gives it motion and a name.

    What does it mean?

    Nothing needs repeating yet: what counts at this age is hearing the word said with warmth, over and over, attached to something worth watching. Words that arrive during genuine play get processed as good news, and good news is remembered.

    What does the child need to know?

    The order matters: roll the real ball first, then show the card, or roll after the card — either way, play leads and language follows. Replies, when they come months from now, will arrive on their own schedule; nothing needs prompting today.

    Why this matters

    First words are overwhelmingly the things babies see most, and a ball tops many lists. Every warm repetition now is a deposit in the account your baby will draw on when speech starts — deposits made in laughter earn the best interest.

    What it teaches

    Object recognition, visual tracking of moving targets, reach-and-grab aim, and word-pleasure pairing — the emotional side of vocabulary that makes words worth saying later.

    Words to learn

    ballrollroundbouncygoneagain

    Say this to your child

    “"Ball! Here is the picture ball, all round and bright. Now watch — a real ball, rolling across the floor... and it stopped. Did you see? Rolling balls, still balls — they are all ball. What a good word."”

    Step by step

    1. Settle your baby and show the card at close range with its name: "Ball. Round and ready for a game."
    2. Let the picture earn a good look — then fetch a real ball: big, light, clean, and bigger than their fist.
    3. Roll it slowly across the mat within full view, saying "ball" once as it moves, and let it stop naturally.
    4. Wait. A reach, a bat, a shout of delight — answer whichever arrives with a warm "yes, ball!" and let hands meet the ball.
    5. Close by returning to the card for one final look, so the word has been heard at the picture and at the game.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a simple bright ball — say that much. The live noticing: did the eyes follow the roll to the end, and did the gaze come back to the card after the game? That round trip is the whole lesson, happening or not happening, right in front of you.

    Ask your child

    Watch the circuit: picture, world, picture — where does the trip break down today? Does the reach aim for the card or the ball? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if the rolling ball or the still one holds your eyes longer."

    What your child can say or do

    Eyes locked on the full roll, a two-handed grab that lands on the ball, a squeal at the first movement, or babbling that starts up mid-game — ba-ba noises during ball play are not coincidence; the sound and the word are neighbours.

    Out in the real world

    Balls are everywhere once you list them: the one clipped to the pram, the big therapy ball at baby group, the dog’s tennis ball. One word at each sighting keeps this card running all week without another session.

    Try it together

    Stop-and-go roll: roll the ball a short way, say "ball", let it rest, then roll it back. The stop is as important as the go — each restart is another naming moment, and your baby learns that games have a rhythm words can live inside.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the real ball actually roll today, and did you say the word once per roll rather than on loop? One word per event is what makes each naming land — narrating non-stop buries the word you are planting.

    Parent tips

    If your baby grabs for the card itself, let them hold it with you — crinkling and gumming a corner is real learning at this age. Rotate which ball you use so the word attaches to round things in general, not one exact toy.

    Staying safe

    Balls for this age are big, light and unmarked — nothing smaller than their fist, nothing with a broken seam, nothing retrieved from under the sofa mid-session. The card returns to adult hands after any shared holding.

    This lesson pairs with the Ball flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Words & Familiar Things (Infant 2).

    Cup — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Of everything in your house, this may be the object your baby knows best — it appears at every single feed, which makes its name some of the most valuable vocabulary you can offer. This lesson pins the word to the routine that already runs your day.

    What is this?

    A cup is a drinking vessel, and your baby has studied it in action for months — lifted, tipped, emptied, refilled. The card gives the daily prop a still portrait; the routine supplies everything else.

    What does it mean?

    Words attached to routines get hundreds of free rehearsals: every feed is another performance of cup. And because the routine is deeply familiar, the word lands on ground that is already prepared — no explanation needed, only repetition in the same warm voice.

    What does the child need to know?

    One word, one tone, many moments — that is the whole method. The card at quiet time, the real cup at mealtime, the word said the same way in both places. Your baby is learning that a word belongs to the thing wherever it appears, not to one picture.

    Why this matters

    High-frequency routine words are the spine of a first vocabulary: they repeat, they matter emotionally, and they attach to events the baby can predict. Cup will be heard, seen and soon perhaps reached-for every single day — word and world in permanent partnership.

    What it teaches

    Word-object mapping across settings, anticipation of routines, mealtime attention, and listening memory — hearing one word in many places until it becomes portable.

    Words to learn

    cupdrinkmilkmoreemptyfull

    Say this to your child

    “"Cup! Here is the picture cup. And here comes our real cup, arriving for milk, just like always. Card cup, feeding cup — same word, same cup, every day. You know this friend better than anyone."”

    Step by step

    1. At a calm moment, show the card at close range and name it: "Cup. Your old friend the cup."
    2. Trace its outline with one finger — the round body, the handle if it has one — while your baby watches.
    3. At the next feed, say "cup" in the identical voice before the real cup arrives, then bring the cup into view.
    4. Let the feed proceed normally; the word has been planted and the routine will water it.
    5. Keep the pairing going daily — card at quiet time, word at feed time — and listen for babbling that starts to sound like an answer.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a simple, clear cup — say that much and no more. The live noticing: when the word comes before the object at feed time, does your baby’s attention jump ahead to where the cup always appears? Prediction is the visible half of vocabulary.

    Ask your child

    Watch the routine: does the word "cup" collect a look before the object arrives? Does the card itself get a calmer, longer study than it used to? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if you already know what happens after the word cup."

    What your child can say or do

    A head-turn to the usual cup-spot at the word, excited leg-thumping as the feed begins, babbling bursts around mealtimes, or hands that reach for the real cup now as well as the card — reaching for the named thing is a milestone wearing ordinary clothes.

    Out in the real world

    Cups fill every room: the kitchen shelf, the bath, the café table, grandma’s house. Each sighting can carry one warm "cup" — and unlike most vocabulary, this word pays rent daily, at every drink, for years.

    Try it together

    Two-cup surprise: show the card, then bring two different real cups into view one after the other, saying "cup" for each. Different shapes, same word — your baby gets an early lesson that names cover a whole family of things.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the word "cup" sound the same at card time and at feed time today? Consistency of voice is the invisible ingredient — it is what lets your baby trust that one sound means one thing.

    Parent tips

    If feeds are rushed or fussy, drop the feed-time version and keep only the card — never let the word arrive with stress attached. The pairing works because both ends are pleasant; protect that, and the vocabulary builds itself.

    Staying safe

    The cup you name stays cool and baby-appropriate — hot drinks ride on high shelves, never across a feeding lap. The card itself stays out of the splash zone; a card that has met the milk goes straight to the recycling.

    This lesson pairs with the Cup flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Words & Familiar Things (Infant 2).

    Spoon — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Meals are the busiest classroom in the house, and the spoon is its best prop. This lesson shows you how to teach the word without turning any meal into a lesson.

    What is this?

    A spoon is the scoop that carries food, and your baby has watched it fly between bowl and mouth for months. The card gives the tool a calm portrait before the busy version appears at the table.

    What does it mean?

    Not every word needs a sit-down session. Ambient repetition — the word said casually, in passing, at the real moment — is how much of early vocabulary actually lands. The card prepares the sound; the meals supply the rehearsals.

    What does the child need to know?

    The card can simply sit on the table, safely out of grab range, while you point at it once, mid-meal, and say "spoon" without ceremony. Low drama is the point: casual meetings teach your baby that words are part of ordinary life, not performances.

    Why this matters

    Words that appear in their natural habitat stick differently than words on paper alone. Spoon at the table, spoon in the card, spoon in the drawer — each meeting in a new place tells your baby the word is bigger than any one sighting.

    What it teaches

    Tool-word learning, casual repetition tolerance (not every naming needs a response), mealtime attention, and the connection between objects, actions and their names.

    Words to learn

    spoonfoodtastyscoopopen wideyum

    Say this to your child

    “"Spoon! Here is the picture spoon. And look — our spoon is working right now, flying from bowl to mouth. Scoop, lift, here it comes. Spoon is a busy word. It works at every single meal."”

    Step by step

    1. At quiet time, show the card at close range: "Spoon. The little scoop that brings the food."
    2. Trace the long handle and the bowl end, once each, while your baby studies the shape.
    3. Prop the card safely out of reach at the next meal — on a shelf, a windowsill, anywhere visible but ungrabbable.
    4. Once during the meal, tap towards it casually and say "spoon" — no pause in the meal, no spotlight, no repetition.
    5. Repeat at several meals across the week; the ordinariness is what makes the word feel like furniture.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a simple, friendly spoon — say that much. The live noticing: does your baby glance between the card at its post and the working spoon during the meal? Words that live in two places start gathering their meanings from both.

    Ask your child

    Watch the casual tap: does a single quiet "spoon" earn any look at all — or none, which is equally fine? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if the word works better at the start of the meal or in the middle of it."

    What your child can say or do

    A flick of the eyes towards the card at the tap, mouth-opening when the real spoon approaches, a hand reaching past the card towards the actual food, or no reaction at all — ambient teaching expects nothing and often gets everything a week later.

    Out in the real world

    Spoon sightings run all day: the weaning spoons in the drawer, the big serving spoon at dinner, the spoon in the play kitchen. Each one can carry a passing word — and the more places the word lives, the faster it becomes real.

    Try it together

    Spoon flights: once a day, let the real spoon make one theatrical flight from bowl to your own mouth, with the word attached. One flight, one word, done. Tiny, silly, daily — this is how mealtime words get their wings.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the word "spoon" get said at a real meal today without the meal pausing for it? If yes, the ambient method is working exactly as designed — vocabulary woven through the day, not bolted onto it.

    Parent tips

    Do not escalate into drilling — no "say spoon!", no waiting for echoes. At 4–6 months the reply is months away and pressure now only adds noise. The card at the table can stay for a week; novelty fades, repetition stays.

    Staying safe

    The card’s seat at the table is chosen for reach: visible from your baby’s chair, impossible to grab, nowhere near hot plates. Real spoons for babies stay soft-tipped and adult-held until feeding time makes them working tools.

    This lesson pairs with the Spoon flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Words & Familiar Things (Infant 2).

    Bottle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    If your baby is bottle-fed, this card names the most familiar object in their world — the thing they know better than anything else in it, arriving with a name at last. This lesson keeps it gentle and routine-shaped.

    What is this?

    A bottle is the feeding vessel your baby knows intimately: held, tipped, warm, arriving at the best moments of the day. The card turns that deeply loved object into a picture that can be named.

    What does it mean?

    Comfort-and-food words are heavyweight vocabulary: they arrive when your baby is relaxed, attentive and emotionally wide open. Bottle is not just a label; it is the name of a feeling that happens several times a day.

    What does the child need to know?

    Show the card in the minute before a feed, say the word softly, and let the beloved routine carry it — your only job is not overdoing it. One warm word before the milk is worth ten repetitions after it.

    Why this matters

    Comfort words build the emotional foundation of language: they teach your baby that sounds can predict good things. A baby who brightens at "bottle" has learned what words are for — announcements of the best parts of life.

    What it teaches

    Word-ritual association, anticipation and recognition, emotional security through naming, and the earliest understanding that sounds can stand for things not yet visible.

    Words to learn

    bottlemilkwarmtime forhungrydrink

    Say this to your child

    “"Bottle! Here is the picture bottle. And look — here comes the real one, warm and ready, just for you. Bottle time, little one. The best word at the best moment. Hello, bottle. Welcome back."”

    Step by step

    1. Just before the feed begins — not during, not after — show the card at close range and say "bottle" once, softly.
    2. Let your baby look at the picture while the real feeling of feeding-time arrives; the card rides the moment.
    3. Then bring the actual bottle into view: "Here it is." Picture, then reality, seconds apart, every feed if you like.
    4. Keep your voice at feed-volume — low, warm, unhurried; this word should never shout.
    5. Over days, watch for the brightening at the word alone; when that arrives, the word has done its deep work.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a simple, clear baby bottle — say that much. The live noticing is emotional: what changes in your baby’s body between the card, the word, and the real bottle arriving? Feed-time vocabulary shows up as whole-body recognition, not pointing.

    Ask your child

    Watch the order: does the word alone start to pull attention before the bottle appears? Does the card get a soft look or an impatient one? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if you think the picture is the same promise as the real thing."

    What your child can say or do

    Whole-face brightening at the word, rooting and wriggling as the feed approaches, hands opening and closing towards the real bottle, or contented sucking noises aimed at the card — comfort vocabulary shows its work in the body first.

    Out in the real world

    Bottle moments happen several times a day in bottle-feeding families — every one is a natural replay. And breastfed babies can borrow the lesson too: the card simply names a feeding vessel they will meet in daily life soon enough.

    Try it together

    Bottle countdown: as you prepare the feed, hold the card where your baby can see it and let them watch the bottle being made — picture in view, word said once, then the real thing. Waiting becomes part of the word’s story.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the word arrive before the milk today, and did it stay soft? Sequence and tone are the entire technique — the word must always be the herald of the good thing, never a commentator on it.

    Parent tips

    If your baby is too hungry at feed time to look at anything, show the card slightly earlier — during preparation, not presentation. Never wedge the card into a crying moment; this word only works in happiness.

    Staying safe

    Prepared bottles follow your usual safe-handling rules — temperature-checked, fresh, held by you. The card stays out of the feed zone entirely: no paper near the milk, and the card goes away before the feeding hold begins.

    This lesson pairs with the Bottle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Words & Familiar Things (Infant 2).

    Apple — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The apple is a first-words classic: an object your baby has seen in the fruit bowl since birth, with a shape and colour that make the picture a joy to look at. This lesson brings card and fruit together.

    What is this?

    An apple is a round tree fruit that lives in kitchens and lunchboxes, red or green. Your baby cannot eat one yet — but learning its name now means the word is waiting when the first apple slice arrives.

    What does it mean?

    Kitchen words grow fast because the kitchen is where babies already look: high chairs face the action, and food moves constantly. Naming a food before the baby eats it builds a bridge — when weaning starts, apple will be an old friend wearing a new form.

    What does the child need to know?

    Hold the fruit right next to the card and invite your baby’s eyes to travel between them — one word, happily covering both. Then put the fruit away and finish with the picture. No tasting today; the mouth learns this word months from now, at its own milestone.

    Why this matters

    Every object your baby can name before they can use it arrives at its milestone with a head start. The apple slice at weaning will come attached to a word, a shape and a memory of looking — three advantages, all planted in sessions like this one.

    What it teaches

    Picture-world transfer, size and colour comparison, fruit-bowl familiarity, and listening vocabulary that will surface again at first tastes.

    Words to learn

    appleredroundshinyfruit bowlcrunchy

    Say this to your child

    “"Apple! Here is the picture apple, red and shiny. And here is a real one from our fruit bowl — big, round, heavy. Picture apple, real apple, one word for both. Soon you will hold one of these yourself. What a day that will be."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card at close range and name it warmly: "Apple. A shiny red apple."
    2. Give the picture its look — then fetch a real apple, washed, whole and unbruised.
    3. Hold fruit beside card at matched height and say "apple" once; let the eyes make their own trips between them.
    4. Rotate the real apple slowly in your hand — a new angle, the same apple — then bring the card back into view.
    5. Finish on the card, and put the fruit back where it lives; the lesson ends with the picture getting the last word.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a bright round apple — say that much. The live noticing: how many gaze-trips between card and fruit today, and did the real apple’s shine or weight collect extra looking? Transfer is quiet work; count crossings, not reactions.

    Ask your child

    Watch the comparison: does the gaze settle on the fruit, the card, or travel? Does the real apple’s smell earn attention when it comes close? Wonder aloud: "I wonder which apple you think is the real one — I know, but I am curious how you see it."

    What your child can say or do

    Steady back-and-forth looking, fingers opening towards the real apple, a lean-in at the fruit’s smell, or babbling that pops up during the naming — all of it counts, and none of it needs to become tasting.

    Out in the real world

    Apples appear constantly: the fruit bowl, your snack, the market stall, the neighbour’s tree. One word at each sighting turns the whole neighbourhood into this card’s practice room.

    Try it together

    Bowl guest of honour: once a day, lift the apple from the fruit bowl, greet it by name to your baby, and return it. Thirty seconds of ceremony, no card required — the world’s most patient picture book, open on the counter.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the real apple stand beside the card today, and did the session end on the picture? The discipline of one-word-two-forms is what keeps kitchen vocabulary crisp instead of mushy.

    Parent tips

    If your baby mouths towards the fruit, acknowledge the interest warmly and keep the apple out of reach — the interest itself is the learning. Choose the shiniest apple in the bowl for sessions; gloss pulls baby eyes.

    Staying safe

    Whole apples are hard as stones and stay far from reaching hands — and when solids arrive months from now, apple is served cooked, grated or as a thin slice, never as a chunk. Today, the fruit is a prop, not a snack.

    This lesson pairs with the Apple flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Words & Familiar Things (Infant 2).

    Banana — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Banana has real character as a first word goes: silly to say, strange to look at, and famous for the peel. This lesson lets the comedy do the teaching.

    What is this?

    A banana is a long, curved yellow fruit that arrives in its own wrapper. Your baby may know its smell from family breakfasts; the card gives the fruit a portrait, and the peel gives the lesson its show.

    What does it mean?

    Funny-sounding words get repeated by the grown-ups who enjoy them, and repetition is everything at this age. Words that make parents smile get said more warmly, more often, and with more melody — banana is a word babies hear loved.

    What does the child need to know?

    The ceremony is in the peel: unwrap a real banana strip by strip as you say the word, letting the reveal build. Your baby cannot eat it yet, and does not need to — the unfolding is fascinating all by itself, and the word rides along with the drama.

    Why this matters

    Words with personality survive. Banana has sound-play built in — ba-na-na — and babies soaked in its syllables for months often say some version of it astonishingly early. You are not teaching the word; you are marinating your baby in it.

    What it teaches

    Sound-play exposure (syllable rhythm), anticipation through slow reveal, smell and sight pairing, and the social joy of a word that makes both of you happy.

    Words to learn

    bananayellowpeelopensmellnana

    Say this to your child

    “"Banana! Ba-na-na — what a funny word. Here is the picture banana, curved like a smile. And here is a real one — watch it open, slowly, slowly... there! Yellow inside, yellow outside. Banana is the silliest, best word."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card at close range and give the word its full silly voice: "Banana! A long, yellow, funny banana."
    2. Trace the crescent shape on the card with one finger — there is no other fruit shaped quite like this.
    3. Fetch a real banana and peel it slowly, a strip at a time, saying "banana" as each fold comes down.
    4. Hold the opened fruit briefly near your baby — the smell is part of the lesson — then bring the card back for the final look.
    5. Put the banana away for the family’s breakfast and close the session with the picture; the fruit served its purpose.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a cheerful banana in its bold simple style — say that much. The live noticing: during the slow peel, where are your baby’s eyes — the unfolding fruit, the falling strip, your face? The peel pulls attention three ways, and all three are fine.

    Ask your child

    Watch the show: does the slow build hold attention longer than the finished fruit? Does the smell earn a lean or a wide-eyed still? Wonder aloud: "I wonder which part you like best — the word, the smell, or the unfolding."

    What your child can say or do

    Fixed staring at the peeling hands, a wriggle of anticipation as each strip falls, a sniff-and-lean at the opened fruit, or early babbles that echo the word’s rhythm — na-na noises during banana week are more than coincidence.

    Out in the real world

    Bananas live on countertops and in lunchboxes, and they will star in your baby’s own weaning months soon. Every family banana is a replay now — mash practice later, word practice today.

    Try it together

    Peek-a-peel: with the card hidden behind a real banana, reveal it bit by bit — a corner first, then the whole picture — saying the word when it appears. The peel’s logic, played with paper and fruit together.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did you say the word slowly enough to enjoy it, and did the peel actually take its time? Speed is the enemy of this lesson; the whole method is a slow reveal in a warm voice.

    Parent tips

    If the word makes you grin, say it more — your enjoyment is the curriculum. Vary the voice across days: whisper banana, sing banana, stretch banana. The syllables are elastic and your baby is listening to all of it.

    Staying safe

    Real bananas stay with the grown-ups until weaning months — a whole banana is a binding hazard, and the peel goes straight to the bin, not the exploring hand. The session banana returns to the fruit bowl or the breakfast plate.

    This lesson pairs with the Banana flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Words & Familiar Things (Infant 2).

    Cat — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Cats fill books, streets, screens and half of all baby toys, which makes cat a genuinely useful early word. This lesson gives it a picture and a sound your baby can hold onto.

    What is this?

    A cat is a small, soft, whiskered animal — famous for independence and for one very sayable sound. Whether a real cat patrols your hallway or not, the word travels through your baby’s whole world of books and toys.

    What does it mean?

    Animal words carry sound-effects for free, and sound is a memory hook: meow gives the word a second handle, a musical one. Babies remember words better when the word arrives with a noise their own mouth can almost try.

    What does the child need to know?

    Add the meow — soft, not startling — and wait. Any reaction counts as participation: a startle, a grin, a kick, a babble. If a real cat strolls past later in the day, the word gets one more outing; the replay in the wild is where it becomes permanent.

    Why this matters

    Animal words are usually among the first a child understands, because animals move, make noise and star in everything aimed at babies. Cat is the friendly ambassador of that whole family — small, familiar-shaped, and equipped with its own soundtrack.

    What it teaches

    Animal recognition, sound-word pairing, reaction-to-novelty (startle that settles is healthy development), and memory hooks through repeated sound effects.

    Words to learn

    catmeowsoftwhiskerskittygentle

    Say this to your child

    “"Cat! Here is the picture cat, with its pointy ears and whiskers. A cat says meow — can you hear it? Meow, meow, soft and friendly. Cats are everywhere — in books, on the street, on your sock. Cat is a word worth knowing."”

    Step by step

    1. Start with the card at close range, saying the name warmly: "Cat! A soft, whiskery cat."
    2. Trace the ears and whiskers on the card while your baby studies the face.
    3. Add the sound: a soft, friendly "meow" — then wait, and let whatever happens back be the reply.
    4. If interest holds, run the pair again: the word, the meow, a beat of quiet. Two rounds is plenty.
    5. Later in the day, replay it in the wild — a cat on the street, a cat in a book, a toy cat on the shelf — with the same word and sound.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a friendly cat in clear simple features — say that much. The live noticing: what does the meow earn? A blink, a startle that melts into a smile, a leg-kick — reactions to animal sounds are real developmental information.

    Ask your child

    Watch the sound: does the meow collect more attention than the picture alone? Does the reaction shrink the second time as the sound becomes familiar? Wonder aloud: "I wonder when the meow will stop being a surprise and start being a joke."

    What your child can say or do

    A startle-blink at the first meow, a gummy grin by the third, arm-waves or leg-kicks in reply, or a babble that tries out the same shape of sound — m-m-m noises after cat sessions are your baby rehearsing the family of sounds.

    Out in the real world

    Cats prowl through daily life: the neighbour’s cat on the wall, cats in every picture book, the cat on the milk carton. Each sighting is a replay — word, sound, done — until cat becomes permanently yours.

    Try it together

    Meow-and-wait: say the word, do the meow, then pause with an expectant face. Whatever your baby offers — a sound, a movement, a stare — answer warmly as if it were conversation. Because at this age, it is.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the meow stay soft, and did you wait after it rather than filling the silence? The waiting is where your baby’s turn lives; fill it and the conversation dies before it starts.

    Parent tips

    If your home has a real cat, the card gains a live co-star — but keep sessions calm and the animal always in control of its own participation. No cat at home? Books and toys carry the word perfectly well.

    Staying safe

    Real cats and babies meet only under close supervision, with the cat free to leave and claws out of the equation — the card carries the lesson; the animal is a guest, never a prop. Keep the meow gentle: startled babies learn less.

    This lesson pairs with the Cat flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Words & Familiar Things (Infant 2).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FIRST WORDS & FAMILIAR THINGS · AGES 4–6 MONTHS

    Dog — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Dogs bring their own sound and action to every card session: barking and tail-wagging are easy to act out. This lesson turns the dog card into a tiny performance your baby will wait for.

    What is this?

    A dog is a four-legged, tail-wagging, often noisy friend — the animal your baby is most likely to meet in real life, on leads, in parks and on doorsteps. The card gives the word a face; your performance gives it everything else.

    What does it mean?

    Sound plus action gives a word two handles to hold: the ears remember woof, the eyes remember the wag. Multi-channel words survive better in baby memory — and dog, performed with commitment, is the most multi-channel word in the set.

    What does the child need to know?

    Do the woof, then pat your own head like floppy ears or wag an imaginary tail — then wait. Any reaction is participation: a jolt, a laugh, a kick. Dogs vary in real life — big, small, loud, quiet — so say that out loud across the week: all of them are dog.

    Why this matters

    Dogs are often the first animal a baby names in the wild, because the wild is full of them. A word with a built-in sound gives your baby something to recognise before speech: the day your baby turns towards a real bark and brightens, the card will be working.

    What it teaches

    Sound recognition, action-word pairing, reaction-and-recovery to loud sounds, and generalisation — one word covering many different-looking dogs.

    Words to learn

    dogwoofwagtailbigsmall

    Say this to your child

    “"Dog! Here is the picture dog, tail going wiggle-waggle. A dog says woof! Woof, woof! Big dogs, small dogs, loud dogs, quiet dogs — they all say woof, and they are all called dog. What a useful word this is."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card at close range with a bright voice: "Dog! A happy dog with a waggy tail."
    2. Point out the tail on the card and give it a wiggle with your fingertip — dogs are defined by that wag.
    3. Do your best woof — two of them, playful not percussive — then wait for whatever comes back.
    4. Add the body: pat your head like floppy ears or wag your hand like a tail, pairing sound with movement.
    5. Across the week, replay the word at every real or pictured dog, noting that huge hounds and tiny lapdogs share one name.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a happy dog with its tongue out and tail up — say that much. The live noticing: does the woof earn a bigger reaction than the picture alone? And does the recovery — surprise melting into interest — get faster across the week? That speed-up is learning.

    Ask your child

    Watch the performance: which part collects your baby — the sound, the action, or the picture? Does a real dog’s bark out in the world pull a look now? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if you are starting to know this word before it even lands."

    What your child can say or do

    A jolt at the first woof that turns into watching, full kicks of delight at the tail-wag hand, babbling that copies the b-sound, or a head-turn towards real barks on walks — the last one is the milestone hiding in plain hearing.

    Out in the real world

    Dogs are everywhere: on leads at the park, behind garden fences, in every third picture book. Each real dog is a replay — and saying "dog" about a great dane and a chihuahua in the same afternoon is generalisation, the quiet superpower of words.

    Try it together

    Woof-peek: hide the card behind your back, do a small woof, then reveal the dog with "there he is!" Repeat until the giggles or the yawns arrive. The sound predicts the reveal — your baby is learning prediction, the root of all games.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the word cover more than one dog this week — two sizes, two barks, one name? If yes, generalisation is happening; if not, next walk is the classroom and it is already scheduled.

    Parent tips

    Commit to the performance — a shy woof teaches half a word. If your baby startles strongly, halve the volume and double the smile; the goal is surprise with recovery, not fright. Vary dog sizes in books across the week.

    Staying safe

    Real dogs stay at arm’s length and behind their owners’ control — the word is learned freely, the animal is met only with permission and calm. If a passing bark startles your baby, name it warmly and move on; recovery is part of the lesson.

    This lesson pairs with the Dog flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Words & Familiar Things (Infant 2).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FIRST WORDS & FAMILIAR THINGS · AGES 4–6 MONTHS

    Bird — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Birds are among the first moving things a baby notices outdoors — flashes of motion at the window that nothing else explains. This lesson gives that fascination a name.

    What is this?

    A bird is a small feathered animal that flies, hops and sings. The card shows one clearly; the window supplies the live version; and the word — bird — connects the two across your baby’s whole day.

    What does it mean?

    Words that land on things your baby has already watched are the fastest route into language: the memory exists, and the word simply moves in. Birds have the added gift of motion — the eyes found them long before the word did, which means attention was never the problem.

    What does the child need to know?

    Then take the session to the window and watch together in real quiet. A single passing bird, named at the moment it moves, outweighs any number of rounds at the card.

    Why this matters

    Window words — bird, sun, car, tree — are your baby’s first reach past the arm’s-length world. They prove that language describes things too far away to touch, and they turn every windowsill into a reading of the day’s news.

    What it teaches

    Distant-object naming, motion tracking, word-event association at real moments, and the habit of shared looking — two people watching the same small wonder.

    Words to learn

    birdflytweetup highwindowthere

    Say this to your child

    “"Bird! Here is the picture bird, with its little wings. Now let us look outside — up in the sky, out on the branch... birds fly out there, fast and free. Did you see one? Bird is the word for all of them."”

    Step by step

    1. Lay the card out at close range and introduce it: "Bird! A small bird with feathers."
    2. Trace the wing on the card and flap your hand gently — birds are their flying.
    3. Move to the window with your baby settled against you, and simply watch together for a while.
    4. If a bird appears or a branch moves, say "bird" once, at the moment of the sighting — then let the quiet return.
    5. Close with the card back at your lap, so the word has lived in both places today: page and pane.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a small friendly bird in bold simple shape — say that much. The live noticing: what does your baby watch at the window — the birds, the leaves, the light? Naming what they actually track, not what you hoped they would, is the honest version of this lesson.

    Ask your child

    Watch the window: does a moving bird collect the gaze faster than a still scene? Does the word earn a look even when no bird shows? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if you would spot the bird before I do if your eyes were quicker — some days I think they are."

    What your child can say or do

    A locked stare on a flying bird, whole-body stillness at the window, squeals when wings move, or a patient study of empty branches — window watching is its own activity, and every version of it is language preparation.

    Out in the real world

    Birds are daily guests: on the lawn, at the feeder, crossing the sky on the school run, in the car park at the shops. The word costs one breath per sighting and repays itself for a lifetime.

    Try it together

    Wing-flap echo: at the card, flap your hands like wings and say "fly" as you lift them. Your baby cannot copy yet, but the motion-word pairing sinks in — and one day, a flapping baby at this same card will be your proudest data point.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the window actually happen today, and did you resist narrating every second of it? Shared quiet looking, punctuated by one word at the right moment, is the technique — commentary is its enemy.

    Parent tips

    No birds today? The card still teaches, and the window still works — sky-watching is the ritual, birds are the bonus. Keep a mental note of your baby’s best window hour; every house has one, and it is worth knowing.

    Staying safe

    Window sessions happen in your arms or a supported seat, never propped against the glass — and screens stay closed if the baby is within reach of the latch. Balconies and open windows are grown-up territory; the lesson ends at the pane.

    This lesson pairs with the Bird flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Words & Familiar Things (Infant 2).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FIRST WORDS & FAMILIAR THINGS · AGES 4–6 MONTHS

    Car — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    All day, cars stream past the window — and for many families this ends up the most-said word in the whole set. This lesson starts the habit with a card that moves.

    What is this?

    A car is a wheeled vehicle that carries people — bright, fast and permanently fascinating from a window. The card gives one a portrait; the lesson gives it motion, sound and a name said at the moment it passes.

    What does it mean?

    Movement plus sound equals attention: a sliding card and a vroom collect a baby gaze like nothing still can. And passing cars are a gift to vocabulary — they arrive, they get named, they leave, and the word stays behind, ready for the next one.

    What does the child need to know?

    Send the card gliding through the air like a car going by, then give it one vroom. Watch which things your baby tracks longest — that preference is your baby announcing what they love, and love is the engine of every word that follows.

    Why this matters

    Car will be heard hundreds of times in your baby’s first years — on walks, in the pushchair, from the window. Giving the word a picture and a sound now means every future sighting lands on prepared ground. Few words offer this much free repetition.

    What it teaches

    Motion tracking, sound-word pairing, interest-mapping (noticing what your baby chooses to watch), and the habit of naming passing events in real time.

    Words to learn

    carvroomfastslowgostop

    Say this to your child

    “"Car! Here is the picture car, all ready to go. Watch it drive... vroom! Off it goes, fast as anything. And look outside — real cars, going past the window, one after another. Car is a very busy word."”

    Step by step

    1. Bring the card up close and open with the name: "Car! A bright, speedy car."
    2. Point out the wheels — cars are their wheels — and give them a spin with your fingertip.
    3. Hold the card up and slide it slowly through the air, side to side, like a car passing the window.
    4. Say "vroom" once at the end of the pass — then park the card on your lap and let it rest there.
    5. Later, at any real window or street corner, name the passing cars the same way: one word per car, not per minute.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a bright simple car — say that much. The live noticing: does the sliding card hold the gaze the whole way, and do real cars collect a look at the window? Tracking a moving vehicle is exactly what these weeks are building.

    Ask your child

    Watch the pass: does the gaze follow the slide or lose it at speed? Which wins today — fast passes, slow passes, or the parked card? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if you like the going or the stopping better."

    What your child can say or do

    Eyes glued to the full slide, a startle-grin at the vroom, kicking that starts when the card launches, or a head-turn towards real traffic sounds — the last one means the word has left the card and moved into the world.

    Out in the real world

    Cars never stop coming: the school run, the delivery van, the neighbour reversing. Each pass is a one-word replay, and the pushchair becomes a moving classroom wherever you walk.

    Try it together

    Slow and speedy: slide the card twice — once painfully slow ("sloooow car"), once quick ("fast car!") — and watch which pass earns more. You are not just naming; you are finding out what kind of motion your baby loves, which is data for every future game.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the card actually move today, and did one real passing car get its word? The sliding is what makes the picture mean motion; the street replay is what makes the word mean car.

    Parent tips

    Vary the slide’s direction across days — left to right, then right to left — so both directions get tracking work. If the vroom delights your baby, keep it exactly as it is; do not upgrade to louder. This word runs on rhythm, not volume.

    Staying safe

    Street-side naming happens from the pushchair or your arms, well back from the road — the lesson lives at windows and pavements, never kerbsides. The card gets a rest after its flights; bent cards still work, torn ones retire.

    This lesson pairs with the Car flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Words & Familiar Things (Infant 2).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FIRST WORDS & FAMILIAR THINGS · AGES 4–6 MONTHS

    Teddy bear — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Here at the end of the set sits its cosiest word: the bear who may already be your baby’s nightly hug. This lesson makes the introduction and closes the set warmly.

    What is this?

    A teddy bear is a soft toy friend — for many babies, the specific one that lives in the cot or rides in the pram. The card is a portrait of someone already known, which makes this the cosiest word in the collection.

    What does it mean?

    Comfort objects hold emotional weight that turns words into anchors: naming the teddy fuses language with security. And a comfort object that attends card time changes the texture of the whole routine — sessions with teddy feel safe, and safe sessions run longer.

    What does the child need to know?

    Fetch the real bear and stage a formal meeting — fur bear greets picture bear, with your voice doing the introductions. Then let teddy stay for the rest of card time as the resident audience. A card that has been thoroughly loved is a card that has been learned.

    Why this matters

    Ending the set with a comfort word is good design: it closes card time on the feeling you want your baby to keep. Babies who finish sessions warm come back to the next one easily — the ending is the advertisement for tomorrow.

    What it teaches

    Emotional security in learning routines, word-object mapping for a beloved object, touch-and-look pairing, and ritual-building — the same warm sequence, repeated until it is a habit.

    Words to learn

    teddybearsofthugfriendnight-night

    Say this to your child

    “"Teddy bear! Look — here is teddy on the card. And here is YOUR teddy, come to meet the picture. Soft teddy, cuddly teddy, friend teddy. Shall we let teddy watch cards with us? Hello, teddy. This is your seat."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card at close range with a warm voice: "Teddy bear! You know this friend."
    2. Let your baby study the picture, then fetch the real teddy and bring it into view beside the card.
    3. Introduce them: "Card teddy, this is real teddy" — and make the real bear wave with your hand doing the work.
    4. Offer the real bear for a touch against your baby’s hands or cheek — soft is the entire point of a bear.
    5. Seat teddy where it can watch the remaining card time, and give it that job at every session from now on.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a soft teddy bear in bold friendly shape — say that much. The live noticing: does the gaze travel between picture bear and fur bear, and does the touch of fur change your baby’s body language? Comfort shows on babies as loosening and leaning.

    Ask your child

    Watch the introduction: does your baby treat the two bears as one friend or two? Does the word alone start to collect a look by week’s end? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if you think the picture bear knows your bear. I like to think they do."

    What your child can say or do

    Looks that swing between card and bear, fingers sinking into fur, a full-body snuggle towards the real bear, or a happy babble at the teddy-voice — the bear tends to produce this set’s biggest reactions, and every one is welcome.

    Out in the real world

    Teddy travels: the cot, the pram, the car seat, the spare at grandma’s house. Each appearance is a replay of the word — and this card often becomes the one your baby "reads" first, months from now, by recognition alone.

    Try it together

    Teddy picks: from today, let the real bear choose which card comes next — your hand operates the paw, the bear "points", and your baby watches the selection ceremony. Rituals like this turn card time from an activity into a story.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the two bears formally meet, and did teddy earn a standing job in the routine? The ritual is what lifts this card above vocabulary into friendship — and warm endings are the best recruitment there is for tomorrow’s session.

    Parent tips

    No teddy in the family? The nearest loved soft thing does the job — the lesson is about naming a cherished object, not this exact bear. Keep the teddy-voice identical across sessions; your baby is memorising that voice as much as the word.

    Staying safe

    Choose a baby-safe bear: no button eyes, no glued decorations, no loose parts, nothing that sheds. If your baby’s sleep bear follows strict sleep-safety rules, card time can borrow a different bear and leave the night friend to its real job.

    This lesson pairs with the Teddy bear flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Words & Familiar Things (Infant 2).
